title: Canada's Regions
summary: Canada's geography: its size and three oceans, the five regions, the national capital, and the ten provinces and three territories with their capitals and what each is known for.

sections.title: Canada's Regions

blocks.text: Canada is the second largest country on earth—10 million square kilometres. Three oceans line Canada's frontiers: the Pacific Ocean in the west, the Atlantic Ocean in the east, and the Arctic Ocean to the north. Along the southern edge of Canada lies the Canada-United States boundary. Both Canada and the U.S.A. are committed to a safe, secure and efficient frontier.

sections.title: The Regions of Canada

blocks.text: Canada includes many different geographical areas and five distinct regions.

sections.title: The National Capital

blocks.text: Ottawa, located on the Ottawa River, was chosen as the capital in 1857 by Queen Victoria, the great-great-grandmother of Queen Elizabeth II. Today it is Canada's fourth largest metropolitan area. The National Capital Region, 4,700 square kilometres surrounding Ottawa, preserves and enhances the area's built heritage and natural environment.
Ottawa's Rideau Canal, once a military waterway, is now a tourist attraction and winter skateway.

sections.title: The Atlantic Provinces

blocks.text: Atlantic Canada's coasts and natural resources, including fishing, farming, forestry and mining, have made these provinces an important part of Canada's history and development. The Atlantic Ocean brings cool winters and cool humid summers.

sections.title: Newfoundland and Labrador

blocks.text: Newfoundland and Labrador is the most easterly point in North America and has its own time zone. In addition to its natural beauty, the province has a unique heritage linked to the sea. The oldest colony of the British Empire and a strategic prize in Canada's early history, the province has long been known for its fisheries, coastal fishing villages and distinct culture. Today off-shore oil and gas extraction contributes a substantial part of the economy. Labrador also has immense hydro-electric resources.

sections.title: Prince Edward Island

blocks.text: Prince Edward Island (P.E.I.) is the smallest province, known for its beaches, red soil and agriculture, especially potatoes. P.E.I. is the birthplace of Confederation, connected to mainland Canada by one of the longest continuous multispan bridges in the world, the Confederation Bridge. Anne of Green Gables, set in P.E.I. by Lucy Maud Montgomery, is a much-loved story about the adventures of a little red-headed orphan girl.

sections.title: Nova Scotia

blocks.text: Nova Scotia is the most populous Atlantic Province, with a rich history as the gateway to Canada. Known for the world's highest tides in the Bay of Fundy, the province's identity is linked to shipbuilding, fisheries and shipping. As Canada's largest east coast port, deep-water and ice-free, the capital, Halifax, has played an important role in Atlantic trade and defence and is home to Canada's largest naval base. Nova Scotia has a long history of coal mining, forestry and agriculture. Today there is also off-shore oil and gas exploration. The province's Celtic and Gaelic traditions sustain a vibrant culture. Nova Scotia is home to over 700 annual festivals, including the spectacular military tattoo in Halifax.

sections.title: New Brunswick

blocks.text: Situated in the Appalachian Range, the province was founded by the United Empire Loyalists and has the second largest river system on North America's Atlantic coastline, the St. John River system. Forestry, agriculture, fisheries, mining, food processing and tourism are the principal industries. Saint John is the largest city, port and manufacturing centre; Moncton is the principal Francophone Acadian centre; and Fredericton, the historic capital. New Brunswick is the only officially bilingual province, and about one-third of the population lives and works in French. The province's pioneer Loyalist and French cultural heritage and history come alive in street festivals and traditional music.

sections.title: Central Canada

blocks.text: More than half the people in Canada live in cities and towns near the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence River in southern Quebec and Ontario, known as Central Canada and the industrial and manufacturing heartland. Southern Ontario and Quebec have cold winters and warm humid summers. Together, Ontario and Quebec produce more than three-quarters of all Canadian manufactured goods.

sections.title: Quebec

blocks.text: Nearly eight million people live in Quebec, the vast majority along or near the St. Lawrence River. More than three-quarters speak French as their first language. The resources of the Canadian Shield have helped Quebec to develop important industries, including forestry, energy and mining. Quebec is Canada's main producer of pulp and paper. The province's huge supply of fresh water has made it Canada's largest producer of hydro-electricity. Quebecers are leaders in cutting-edge industries such as pharmaceuticals and aeronautics. Quebec films, music, literary works and food have international stature, especially in La Francophonie, an association of French-speaking nations. Montreal, Canada's second largest city and the second largest mainly French-speaking city in the world after Paris, is famous for its cultural diversity.

sections.title: Ontario

blocks.text: At more than 12 million, the people of Ontario make up more than one-third of Canadians. The large and culturally diverse population, natural resources and strategic location contribute to a vital economy. Toronto is the largest city in Canada and the country's main financial centre. Many people work in the service or manufacturing industries, which produce a large percentage of Canada's exports. The Niagara region is known for its vineyards, wines and fruit crops. Ontario farmers raise dairy and beef cattle, poultry, and vegetable and grain crops. Founded by United Empire Loyalists, Ontario also has the largest French-speaking population outside of Quebec, with a proud history of preserving their language and culture. There are five Great Lakes located between Ontario and the United States: Lake Ontario, Lake Erie, Lake Huron, Lake Michigan (in the U.S.A.) and Lake Superior, the largest freshwater lake in the world.

blocks.text: Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta are the Prairie Provinces, rich in energy resources and some of the most fertile farmland in the world. The region is mostly dry, with cold winters and hot summers.

sections.title: Manitoba

blocks.text: Manitoba's economy is based on agriculture, mining and hydro-electric power generation. The province's most populous city is Winnipeg, whose Exchange District includes the most famous street intersection in Canada, Portage and Main. Winnipeg's French Quarter, St. Boniface, has Western Canada's largest Francophone community at 45,000. Manitoba is also an important centre of Ukrainian culture, with 14% reporting Ukrainian origins, and the largest Aboriginal population of any province, at over 15%.

sections.title: Saskatchewan

blocks.text: Saskatchewan, once known as the “breadbasket of the world” and the “wheat province,” has 40% of the arable land in Canada and is the country's largest producer of grains and oilseeds. It also boasts the world's richest deposits of uranium and potash, used in fertilizer, and produces oil and natural gas. Regina, the capital, is home to the training academy of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Saskatoon, the largest city, is the headquarters of the mining industry and an important educational, research and technology centre.

sections.title: Alberta

blocks.text: Alberta is the most populous Prairie province. The province, and the world-famous Lake Louise in the Rocky Mountains, were both named after Princess Louise Caroline Alberta, fourth daughter of Queen Victoria. Alberta has five national parks, including Banff National Park, established in 1885. The rugged Badlands house some of the world's richest deposits of prehistoric fossils and dinosaur finds. Alberta is the largest producer of oil and gas, and the oil sands in the north are being developed as a major energy source. Alberta is also renowned for agriculture, especially for the vast cattle ranches that make Canada one of the world's major beef producers.

sections.title: The West Coast

blocks.text: British Columbia is known for its majestic mountains and as Canada's Pacific gateway. The Port of Vancouver, Canada's largest and busiest, handles billions of dollars in goods traded around the world. Warm airstreams from the Pacific Ocean give the B.C. coast a temperate climate.

sections.title: British Columbia

blocks.text: British Columbia (B.C.), on the Pacific coast, is Canada's westernmost province, with a population of four million. The Port of Vancouver is our gateway to the Asia-Pacific. About one-half of all the goods produced in B.C. are forestry products, including lumber, newsprint, and pulp and paper products—the most valuable forestry industry in Canada. B.C. is also known for mining, fishing, and the fruit orchards and wine industry of the Okanagan Valley. B.C. has the most extensive park system in Canada, with approximately 600 provincial parks. The province's large Asian communities have made Chinese and Punjabi the most spoken languages in the cities after English. The capital, Victoria, is a tourist centre and headquarters of the navy's Pacific fleet.

sections.title: The Northern Territories

blocks.text: The Northwest Territories, Nunavut and Yukon contain one-third of Canada's land mass but have a population of only 100,000. There are gold, lead, copper, diamond and zinc mines. Oil and gas deposits are being developed. The North is often referred to as the “Land of the Midnight Sun” because at the height of summer, daylight can last up to 24 hours. In winter, the sun disappears and darkness sets in for three months. The Northern territories have long cold winters and short cool summers. Much of the North is made up of tundra, the vast rocky Arctic plain. Because of the cold Arctic climate, there are no trees on the tundra and the soil is permanently frozen. Some continue to earn a living by hunting, fishing and trapping. Inuit art is sold throughout Canada and around the world.

sections.title: Northwest Territories

blocks.text: The Northwest Territories (N.W.T.) were originally made up in 1870 from Rupert's Land and the North-Western Territory. The capital, Yellowknife (population 20,000), is called the “diamond capital of North America.” More than half the population is Aboriginal (Dene, Inuit and Métis). The Mackenzie River, at 4,200 kilometres, is the second-longest river system in North America after the Mississippi and drains an area of 1.8 million square kilometres.

sections.title: Yukon

blocks.text: Thousands of miners came to the Yukon during the Gold Rush of the 1890s, as celebrated in the poetry of Robert W. Service. Mining remains a significant part of the economy. The White Pass and Yukon Railway opened from Skagway in neighbouring Alaska to the territorial capital, Whitehorse, in 1900 and provides a spectacular tourist excursion across precipitous passes and bridges. Yukon holds the record for the coldest temperature ever recorded in Canada (-63°C).

Mount Logan, located in the Yukon, is the highest mountain in Canada. It is named in honour of Sir William Logan, a world-famous geologist, born in Montreal in 1798 to Scottish immigrant parents. Logan founded and directed the Geological Survey of Canada from 1842 to 1869 and is considered one of Canada's greatest scientists.

sections.title: Nunavut

blocks.text: Nunavut, meaning “our land” in Inuktitut, was established in 1999 from the eastern part of the Northwest Territories, including all of the former District of Keewatin. The capital is Iqaluit, formerly Frobisher Bay, named after the English explorer Martin Frobisher, who penetrated the uncharted Arctic for Queen Elizabeth I in 1576. The 19-member Legislative Assembly chooses a premier and ministers by consensus. The population is about 85% Inuit, and Inuktitut is an official language and the first language in schools.

sections.title: The Canadian Rangers

blocks.text: Canada's vast North brings security and sovereignty challenges. Dealing with harsh weather conditions in an isolated region, the Canadian Rangers, part of the Canadian Forces Reserves (militia), play a key role. Drawing on indigenous knowledge and experience, the Rangers travel by snowmobile in the winter and all-terrain vehicles in the summer from Resolute to the Magnetic North Pole, and keep the flag flying in Canada's Arctic.
The caribou (reindeer) is popular game for hunters and a symbol of Canada's North.

cards.front: After whom were Alberta and Lake Louise named?
cards.back: Princess Louise Caroline Alberta, fourth daughter of Queen Victoria.

cards.front: How many national parks does Alberta have, and when was Banff National Park established?
cards.back: Five national parks, including Banff National Park, established in 1885.

cards.front: What do Alberta's Badlands contain?
cards.back: Some of the world's richest deposits of prehistoric fossils and dinosaur finds.

cards.front: Which province is the largest producer of oil and gas?
cards.back: Alberta. The oil sands in the north are being developed as a major energy source.

cards.front: What is Alberta renowned for in agriculture?
cards.back: Vast cattle ranches that make Canada one of the world's major beef producers.

cards.front: What is Canada's largest and busiest port?
cards.back: The Port of Vancouver, which handles billions of dollars in goods traded around the world. Warm airstreams from the Pacific Ocean give the B.C. coast a temperate climate.

cards.front: Which is Canada's westernmost province, and what is its population?
cards.back: British Columbia, on the Pacific coast, with a population of four million.

cards.front: What share of goods produced in B.C. are forestry products?
cards.back: About one-half, including lumber, newsprint, and pulp and paper products—the most valuable forestry industry in Canada.

cards.front: What is the Okanagan Valley known for?
cards.back: Its fruit orchards and wine industry.

cards.front: Which province has the most extensive park system in Canada?
cards.back: British Columbia, with approximately 600 provincial parks.

cards.front: Which languages are the most spoken in B.C. cities after English?
cards.back: Chinese and Punjabi, because of the province's large Asian communities.

cards.front: What is Victoria known for?
cards.back: The capital of B.C., it is a tourist centre and headquarters of the navy's Pacific fleet.

cards.front: How much of Canada's land mass do the three territories contain, and what is their population?
cards.back: One-third of Canada's land mass, but a population of only 100,000. There are gold, lead, copper, diamond and zinc mines, and oil and gas deposits are being developed.

cards.front: Why is the North called the “Land of the Midnight Sun”?
cards.back: At the height of summer, daylight can last up to 24 hours. In winter, the sun disappears and darkness sets in for three months.

cards.front: What is tundra?
cards.back: The vast rocky Arctic plain. Because of the cold Arctic climate, there are no trees and the soil is permanently frozen.

cards.front: When and from what were the Northwest Territories originally made up?
cards.back: In 1870, from Rupert's Land and the North-Western Territory.

cards.front: Which city is called the “diamond capital of North America”?
cards.back: Yellowknife (population 20,000), the capital of the Northwest Territories.

cards.front: What is the second-longest river system in North America after the Mississippi?
cards.back: The Mackenzie River, at 4,200 kilometres. It drains an area of 1.8 million square kilometres.

cards.front: What share of the Northwest Territories population is Aboriginal?
cards.back: More than half (Dene, Inuit and Métis).

cards.front: When was the Yukon Gold Rush, and whose poetry celebrated it?
cards.back: The 1890s, celebrated in the poetry of Robert W. Service. Thousands of miners came to the Yukon.

cards.front: What is the White Pass and Yukon Railway?
cards.back: A railway opened in 1900 from Skagway in neighbouring Alaska to Whitehorse, now a spectacular tourist excursion.

cards.front: Which territory holds the record for the coldest temperature ever recorded in Canada?
cards.back: Yukon, at -63°C.

cards.front: What is the highest mountain in Canada, and where is it?
cards.back: Mount Logan, in the Yukon, named in honour of Sir William Logan, a world-famous geologist born in Montreal in 1798 who founded and directed the Geological Survey of Canada from 1842 to 1869.

cards.front: What does Nunavut mean, and in what language?
cards.back: “Our land” in Inuktitut.

cards.front: When was Nunavut established, and from what?
cards.back: In 1999, from the eastern part of the Northwest Territories, including all of the former District of Keewatin.

cards.front: What was Iqaluit formerly called, and after whom is it named?
cards.back: Frobisher Bay, named after the English explorer Martin Frobisher, who penetrated the uncharted Arctic for Queen Elizabeth I in 1576.

cards.front: How does Nunavut's Legislative Assembly choose its premier and ministers?
cards.back: The 19-member Legislative Assembly chooses a premier and ministers by consensus.

cards.front: What share of Nunavut's population is Inuit, and what is the status of Inuktitut?
cards.back: About 85% Inuit. Inuktitut is an official language and the first language in schools.

cards.front: Who are the Canadian Rangers?
cards.back: Part of the Canadian Forces Reserves (militia), they play a key role in Canada's North and keep the flag flying in Canada's Arctic.

cards.front: How do the Canadian Rangers travel, and between which points?
cards.back: By snowmobile in the winter and all-terrain vehicles in the summer, from Resolute to the Magnetic North Pole.

quiz.q: How large is Canada?
quiz.why: Canada is the second largest country on earth—10 million square kilometres.

quiz.q: Which ocean lines Canada's northern frontier?
quiz.why: Three oceans line Canada's frontiers: the Pacific in the west, the Atlantic in the east, and the Arctic Ocean to the north.

quiz.q: How many distinct regions does Canada have?
quiz.why: Canada includes many different geographical areas and five distinct regions.

quiz.q: Which of the following is one of the five regions of Canada?
quiz.why: The five regions are the Atlantic Provinces, Central Canada, the Prairie Provinces, the West Coast and the Northern Territories.

quiz.q: Who chose Ottawa as the capital of Canada?
quiz.why: Ottawa was chosen as the capital in 1857 by Queen Victoria.

quiz.q: In what year was Ottawa chosen as the capital?
quiz.why: Ottawa, located on the Ottawa River, was chosen as the capital in 1857 by Queen Victoria.

quiz.q: How many provinces and territories does Canada have?
quiz.why: Canada has ten provinces and three territories.

quiz.q: What is the population of Canada?
quiz.why: Canada has a population of about 34 million people.

quiz.q: What is the capital of Saskatchewan?
quiz.why: Regina is the capital of Saskatchewan; Saskatoon is its largest city.

quiz.q: What is the capital of Nunavut?
quiz.why: The capital of Nunavut is Iqaluit, formerly Frobisher Bay.

quiz.q: What is the capital of Newfoundland and Labrador?
quiz.why: St. John's is the capital of Newfoundland and Labrador; Saint John is the largest city of New Brunswick.

quiz.q: What is the capital of British Columbia?
quiz.why: Victoria is the capital of British Columbia; Vancouver has Canada's largest and busiest port.

quiz.q: What is the capital of New Brunswick?
quiz.why: Fredericton is the historic capital of New Brunswick; Saint John is its largest city and Moncton its principal Francophone Acadian centre.

quiz.q: What is the capital of Quebec?
quiz.why: Québec City is the capital of Quebec; Montreal is Canada's second largest city.

quiz.q: What is the capital of Alberta?
quiz.why: Edmonton is the capital of Alberta.

quiz.q: What is the capital of the Northwest Territories?
quiz.why: The capital of the Northwest Territories is Yellowknife, called the “diamond capital of North America.”

quiz.q: What is the capital of Manitoba?
quiz.why: Winnipeg is the capital and most populous city of Manitoba.

quiz.q: Which of the following is one of the Atlantic Provinces?
quiz.why: The Atlantic Provinces are Newfoundland and Labrador, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.

quiz.q: Which province is the most easterly point in North America and has its own time zone?
quiz.why: Newfoundland and Labrador is the most easterly point in North America and has its own time zone.

quiz.q: Which province was the oldest colony of the British Empire?
quiz.why: Newfoundland and Labrador was the oldest colony of the British Empire and a strategic prize in Canada's early history.

quiz.q: Which is the smallest province in Canada?
quiz.why: Prince Edward Island (P.E.I.) is the smallest province, known for its beaches, red soil and agriculture, especially potatoes.

quiz.q: Which province is the birthplace of Confederation?
quiz.why: P.E.I. is the birthplace of Confederation, connected to mainland Canada by the Confederation Bridge.

quiz.q: Which is the most populous Atlantic Province?
quiz.why: Nova Scotia is the most populous Atlantic Province, with a rich history as the gateway to Canada.

quiz.q: Where are the world's highest tides?
quiz.why: Nova Scotia is known for the world's highest tides in the Bay of Fundy.

quiz.q: Which city is home to Canada's largest naval base?
quiz.why: Halifax, Canada's largest east coast port, is home to Canada's largest naval base.

quiz.q: Which is the only officially bilingual province?
quiz.why: New Brunswick is the only officially bilingual province, and about one-third of the population lives and works in French.

quiz.q: Which city is the principal Francophone Acadian centre of New Brunswick?
quiz.why: Saint John is the largest city; Moncton is the principal Francophone Acadian centre; and Fredericton is the historic capital.

quiz.q: What share of all Canadian manufactured goods do Ontario and Quebec produce together?
quiz.why: Together, Ontario and Quebec produce more than three-quarters of all Canadian manufactured goods.

quiz.q: Which province is Canada's largest producer of hydro-electricity?
quiz.why: Quebec's huge supply of fresh water has made it Canada's largest producer of hydro-electricity; it is also Canada's main producer of pulp and paper.

quiz.q: Which city is the second largest mainly French-speaking city in the world after Paris?
quiz.why: Montreal is Canada's second largest city and the second largest mainly French-speaking city in the world after Paris.

quiz.q: Which is the largest city in Canada and the country's main financial centre?
quiz.why: Toronto is the largest city in Canada and the country's main financial centre.

quiz.q: What is the largest freshwater lake in the world?
quiz.why: Lake Superior is the largest freshwater lake in the world.

quiz.q: Which province has the largest French-speaking population outside of Quebec?
quiz.why: Ontario has the largest French-speaking population outside of Quebec, with a proud history of preserving their language and culture.

quiz.q: Which provinces are the Prairie Provinces?
quiz.why: Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta are the Prairie Provinces, rich in energy resources and some of the most fertile farmland in the world.

quiz.q: In which city is Portage and Main, the most famous street intersection in Canada?
quiz.why: Winnipeg's Exchange District includes the most famous street intersection in Canada, Portage and Main.

quiz.q: Which province has the largest Aboriginal population of any province?
quiz.why: Manitoba has the largest Aboriginal population of any province, at over 15%.

quiz.q: Which province was once known as the “breadbasket of the world”?
quiz.why: Saskatchewan, once known as the “breadbasket of the world” and the “wheat province,” is the country's largest producer of grains and oilseeds.

quiz.q: Where is the training academy of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police?
quiz.why: Regina, the capital of Saskatchewan, is home to the training academy of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.

quiz.q: Which is the most populous Prairie province?
quiz.why: Alberta is the most populous Prairie province.

quiz.q: After whom were Alberta and Lake Louise named?
quiz.why: Alberta and Lake Louise were both named after Princess Louise Caroline Alberta, fourth daughter of Queen Victoria.

quiz.q: Which province is the largest producer of oil and gas?
quiz.why: Alberta is the largest producer of oil and gas, and the oil sands in the north are being developed as a major energy source.

quiz.q: What is Canada's largest and busiest port?
quiz.why: The Port of Vancouver, Canada's largest and busiest, handles billions of dollars in goods traded around the world.

quiz.q: Which province has the most extensive park system in Canada?
quiz.why: B.C. has the most extensive park system in Canada, with approximately 600 provincial parks.

quiz.q: Which languages are the most spoken in B.C. cities after English?
quiz.why: The province's large Asian communities have made Chinese and Punjabi the most spoken languages in the cities after English.

quiz.q: What is the population of the three Northern territories?
quiz.why: The Northwest Territories, Nunavut and Yukon contain one-third of Canada's land mass but have a population of only 100,000.

quiz.q: Why is the North often referred to as the “Land of the Midnight Sun”?
choices: Because the sun never rises in winter
Because at the height of summer, daylight can last up to 24 hours
Because the soil is permanently frozen
quiz.why: The North is called the “Land of the Midnight Sun” because at the height of summer, daylight can last up to 24 hours.

quiz.q: Which city is called the “diamond capital of North America”?
quiz.why: Yellowknife (population 20,000), the capital of the Northwest Territories, is called the “diamond capital of North America.”

quiz.q: What is the second-longest river system in North America after the Mississippi?
quiz.why: The Mackenzie River, at 4,200 kilometres, is the second-longest river system in North America after the Mississippi.

quiz.q: Which territory holds the record for the coldest temperature ever recorded in Canada?
quiz.why: Yukon holds the record for the coldest temperature ever recorded in Canada (-63°C).

quiz.q: What is the highest mountain in Canada?
quiz.why: Mount Logan, located in the Yukon, is the highest mountain in Canada, named in honour of Sir William Logan.

quiz.q: In what year was Nunavut established?
quiz.why: Nunavut was established in 1999 from the eastern part of the Northwest Territories.

quiz.q: What does Nunavut mean in Inuktitut?
quiz.why: Nunavut means “our land” in Inuktitut.

quiz.q: What was Iqaluit formerly called?
quiz.why: The capital is Iqaluit, formerly Frobisher Bay, named after the English explorer Martin Frobisher.

quiz.q: The Canadian Rangers are part of which organization?
quiz.why: The Canadian Rangers, part of the Canadian Forces Reserves (militia), play a key role in Canada's North.
